references.text: The institution of the Passover feast in [ref:2 Mos 12:1-14|Exodus 12:1-14], where God gives the Israelites the command to celebrate Passover (Pesach) and the Feast of Unleavened Bread, which is the background for the feast Luke refers to.
The regulations concerning the Feast of Unleavened Bread (ἑορτὴ τῶν ἀζύμων) in [ref:2 Mos 12:15-20|Exodus 12:15-20], which lasted seven days and was directly linked to the Passover celebration.
In [ref:2 Mos 23:15|Exodus 23:15] the Feast of Unleavened Bread is mentioned as one of the three major pilgrimage feasts in Israel.
In [ref:3 Mos 23:5-8|Leviticus 23:5-8] the detailed regulations for the Passover feast and the Feast of Unleavened Bread are given as part of the Lord's appointed feasts.

The Passover regulations in [ref:5 Mos 16:1-8|Deuteronomy 16:1-8] describe how Passover is to be celebrated in the place the Lord has chosen as a dwelling for His name, linking the feast to Jerusalem.
The parallel passage in [ref:Matt 26:2|Matthew 26:2] where Jesus Himself says that Passover is near and that the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified.

The parallel passage in [ref:Mark 14:1|Mark 14:1] which tells that there were two days until Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread, and that the chief priests and the scribes sought to arrest Jesus by deceit.
In [ref:Joh 11:55|John 11:55] it is mentioned that the Jewish Passover was near, and many went up to Jerusalem to cleanse themselves before the feast – a parallel to Luke's time reference.

In [ref:Joh 13:1|John 13:1] it is told that Jesus knew His hour had come, just before the Passover feast – which emphasizes that Jesus' suffering and death are closely linked to the Passover celebration.
